Neonates emerge with a wet weight at birth of about 125 grams [Wwb = about 125 grams], a modest mass given the species' eventual adult size. This initial measurement is considerably less than the initial wet weight of 143 grams [Ww0 = 143 grams] recorded for the freshly laid egg, reflecting the substantial water loss and metabolic consumption that occurs during embryonic development within the calcareous shell. The altricial nestlings, covered in white down, are entirely dependent on biparental provisioning for warmth and food during the first several weeks post-hatching. This prolonged incubation and early nestling period is energetically demanding for the attending adults, which must hunt frequently to sustain both themselves and the developing chick. This delayed sexual maturation is characteristic of a species that invests heavily in a few offspring rather than many. During this extended pre-reproductive juvenile phase, the immature bird refines its hunting skills, often remaining within or near the natal territory while being fed intermittently by its parents. The acquisition of adult plumage, which takes several years, is another indicator of the bird's slow developmental pace. This slow life-history strategy is typical of apex avian predators that experience low natural mortality once they reach adulthood.

The frequency of reproductive events in the Harpy eagle is exceptionally low, reflecting the high energetic costs of rearing a single chick to independence. Females typically produce one clutch every two years [F_R_i = one clutch every two years], with each clutch containing a maximum of two eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing a maximum of two eggs], though it is rare for both chicks to fledge successfully. This extraordinary reproductive rate, often expressed as a maximum of one successful brood per 730-day interval, is among the lowest documented for any bird of its body mass. The long inter-breeding interval is necessitated by the extended period of post-fledging dependence, during which the young bird continues to rely on adults for food for many months. Under the prevailing ambient conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] in their tropical lowland forest habitat, this slow pace of reproduction is a stable strategy that balances offspring survival against adult condition. Successful nests are often reused or renovated over many seasons, indicating strong site fidelity between these infrequent breeding attempts.

Adult female Harpy eagles attain a truly impressive ultimate wet weight of approximately 8300 grams [Wwi = approximately 8300 grams], making them one of the largest and most powerful eagles in the world. In contrast, adult males are substantially smaller, reaching an ultimate wet weight of about 4450 grams [Wwi = about 4450 grams], a profound sexual size dimorphism that is among the most extreme recorded in any bird of prey. This size difference is thought to reflect niche partitioning, wherein the larger female takes larger prey items while the more agile male focuses on smaller, faster quarry. The maximum longevity recorded for this species under field conditions is approximately 6132 days [am = approximately 6132 days], or just under 17 years, when measured at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], though captive individuals are known to live considerably longer. This extended lifespan, combined with the low reproductive rate, defines the species as a quintessential K-selected organism, highly vulnerable to even modest increases in adult mortality. The massive talons and powerful bill of the female enable her to take substantial arboreal mammals, including sloths and monkeys, which form the core of the species' diet.

The age at which a female Harpy eagle produces her first brood is remarkably late, reflecting the protracted period required to mature and secure a high-quality territory. Field data indicate that the time since birth at first brood is approximately 1642 days [tR = approximately 1642 days], or roughly four and a half years, when maintained at average tropical temperatures of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This delayed onset of breeding is a direct consequence of the species' slow growth rate and the intense competition for suitable nesting sites in the emergent canopy of old-growth forests. Prior to this first breeding attempt, a young adult must locate a mate, defend a large home range, and construct or claim a substantial nest platform. The massive stick nests, often located in the crown of a kapok tree, are used repeatedly across decades, becoming living structures that accumulate moss and epiphytes. This life history strategy, characterized by a very late age at first reproduction, is a common feature of island and tropical raptors that face stable, predictable environments but occupy a high trophic level with limited carrying capacity.
